## Agent operating contract

- Identify the requested outcome, affected components, and evidence needed

## Host-service policy (runit)

This server runs **Artix Linux with glibc**, not Chimera or a musl-based host.
Build and test the server for `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`. An installed musl
cross target or the Codex executable's own musl packaging does not change the
repository's native target. Any separate container portability test must name
its target and must not substitute for the Artix/glibc verification gate.

This host runs **runit** as PID 1. Manage services with `sudo sv <command> <service>` (e.g., `sudo sv restart op-grpc-bridge`). `sv` needs root to read `supervise/ok`.

- `/etc/runit/sv/<service>/run` is the service definition.
- Enabled by a symlink in `/etc/runit/runsvdir/default`.
- Update path: edit the `run` script or install a new binary, then `sudo sv restart <service>`.

Do not edit `/run/runit/service` directly. Do not invoke `runsv`/`runsvdir` by hand. **s6 is legacy**: `service6`, `s6-rc`, `s6-*`, `/run/service` are stale — treat any doc assuming them as historical. Note: `/usr/local/bin/systemctl` on this host is a shim that returns plausible answers — using it masks the deprecation; always use `sv`. Do not use `systemctl` or other foreign service-manager CLIs. Container/app deployment uses D-Bus via `busctl`.

## Network

Network topology, Xray policy, decoy/WARP transport and network-critical
service rules are in `docs/src/operations/network.md`. Read it before any
network work; it is not needed otherwise.


**Owner clarification (2026-09-13): there is no deployment script. Deployment
is btrfs send/receive of the prepared filesystem snapshot.** The release
boundary is the snapshot's contents and the send/receive transfer. Existing
`deploy/` scripts are source/history or preparation tooling; neither
`build-golden.sh` nor `btrfs-layout.sh` defines the current deployment mechanism.
Never hand-copy binaries onto a running host as a deploy step.

**Owner decision (2026-10-23): release is build/preparation only;
`./deploy.sh [--system]` is the deployment entry point.** This supersedes
`activate-golden.sh` and the native `release` activation verb. Deployment
retains Btrfs send/receive into the inactive slot and switches read-only overlays
directly at the declared application targets, not `/opt/op-dbus/current`.
`--system` belongs only to deploy: additionally apply explicitly declared
non-overlay system files to the underlying rootfs, persist the transaction,
and request a graceful runit reboot after successful activation. Never copy
overlay-capable files into base rootfs or overwrite credentials, identities or
runtime data. Preserve existing service wanted/enabled state. Ordinary deploy
does not apply system files or reboot; ordinary rollback restores overlays,
not arbitrary base files. See `deploy/README.md` for the explicit manifest and
approved controller-kit bootstrap boundary. Source implementation does not
establish live deployment: require the durable receipt and postboot evidence.

`deploy/lib/golden/build-golden.sh` only populates and validates
`/opt/op-dbus/golden` from already built artifacts and an already sealed,
persisted catalog. Set `OP_PERSISTED_CATALOG_SOURCE` to use an isolated release
catalog; the script validates and copies it but never reseals it. It does not
create the read-only release snapshot, send
or receive it, activate a received filesystem, install files into the running
host, or restart services. `--golden-only` remains a compatibility alias for
its default behavior; the former `--live-only` and `--no-restart` modes are
retired. Snapshot creation, `btrfs send/receive`, target activation, and any
deliberate target service action are separate operator steps.

```sh
CXXFLAGS="-include cstdint" cargo build --workspace --release
sudo target/release/opblob seal-shm            # explicitly reseal after the build
sudo target/release/opblob persist             # retain the catalog across reboot
```

After builds, explicitly run the freshly built `opblob` to seal the release catalog; bridge startup only consumes sealed blobs and never reseals. For isolated release preparation, use `seal-plugins <new-catalog-dir>` and pass that catalog as `OP_PERSISTED_CATALOG_SOURCE`; publishing live SHM remains part of activation. Match the service's schema-shaping environment. The renamed cognitive code reads `COGNITIVE_*`: `COGNITIVE_QDRANT_URL` defaults to `http://127.0.0.1:6334`, matching the current `deploy/runit/op-grpc-bridge/run`; the historical `COGNITIVE_MCP_QDRANT_URL=http://10.200.0.2:6334` instruction is obsolete. After an explicit GNU-target build, use `target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/opblob`, not an older default-target artifact. Verify the live and persisted catalogs match after activation. Review catalog removals and keep a recoverable copy before a full reseal, which sweeps plugin IDs absent from the build.

The commands above describe build/catalog preparation, not deployment. Do not
infer a live install or restart from a successful build or snapshot preparation.

**Historical clean-baseline activation (2026-09-22; superseded):** the
`/opt/op-dbus/releases/<release-id>` plus `/opt/op-dbus/current` symlink layout
is not the current deployment mechanism. Do not restore that layout or use
its archived operator procedure as deployment authority. The current working
release and its declared slot/overlay state are authoritative. The
`tched-router` runit service still owns the pinned threetched executable on
loopback 8084; the duplicate `zeroclaw` service name remains retired.

## Workspace shape and build

The workspace has **37 member crates under `crates/`, plus the root `op-dbus`
package** (38 workspace packages total). The root package has no application
binary. Binary targets live in members: for example `op-grpc-bridge` and
`op-grants-materializer` in `op-grpc-bridge`, `op-web-server` and `opdbus` in
`op-web`, `opblob` in `op-plugins`, `3tched-fs` (our 3tchedFS schema filesystem,
package `tched-fs`, Rust 2024 edition) in the retained `crates/threetched-fs` directory, and `op-runit-systemctl`/`svd` in
`op-runit-systemctl`. A binary target or runit directory is source inventory,
not proof that it is deployed; reconcile it with `enabled-services` and
`retired-services`. There is no `op-projection` crate. `[patch.crates-io]`
patches only `rovs-openflow` (vendored fork for OF1.5 `packet_type` match at
`vendor/rovs-openflow`). `op-ml`, `op-gallery-gen`, and `op-uds-relay` have manifests under `crates/`
but are outside workspace membership; `op-ml` remains disabled for the ort API breakage (`#ml-fixme`).

**Rust-first: no new Python.** New automation, probes, and helpers go in Rust (`cargo run --bin <name> -p <crate> -- <args>`, a small binary in the relevant crate, or a `cargo-script`-style one-shot) or in shell + POSIX tools (`jq`, `curl`, `busctl`, `sv`). Do not add new `.py` files to the repo. Pre-existing scripts under `scripts/` (`export-llm-sessions-to-notebooklm-sources.py`, `or-fusion-archive.py`, `notebook-sources-cleanup.py`, etc.) are grandfathered — maintain them in place, don't propagate the pattern.

This exception covers running those tools; it does not allow adding new `.py` files to the repo or wiring them into op-dbus services.

All cargo commands run from repo root:

**Owner decision (2026-10-17): JEV owns Cargo model selection and worker
routing.** Do not assign a Cargo-specific model, map caller families to models,
or wrap Cargo in another LLM dispatcher. Use JEV's existing routing without
model overrides. The primary agent stays available for source review,

One Cargo process at a time: if Cargo, rustc or Clippy is running, do not start
another. Workspace-wide builds, checks or tests require an explicit workspace
request. The native target remains `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`; do not install

**Shared Cargo cache ownership (owner repair, 2026-10-23):** run Cargo and its
compiler children as `jeremy` (UID1000), the owner of this checkout and
`target -> /var/lib/cargo-build/odbus-verified`. Never use `sudo cargo` or run a
root execution worker against this cache. Privileged deployment is separate
from compilation. Reuse this shared target for subsequent builds; do not
allocate a fresh per-task target merely to work around access errors.
The cache has inherited owner-specific ACLs for ordinary file creation, not
world-write access; these are defense in depth, not permission to build as root
or rely on ACLs overriding explicit restrictive file modes.
When invoking a toolchain's Cargo binary directly, bind `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` and
`RUSTC`/`RUSTDOC` to that same toolchain so dependency-local rustup overrides
cannot mix compiler versions within the cached build. Preserve JEV routing.

```bash

cargo check -p <crate>
cargo test --workspace --all-targets --all-features
cargo test -p <crate> <test_name>
```

**Frontend — single Vite app, external repo**:

The production UI is **`/srv/git/3tched.com`** (github.com/repr0bated/3tched.com; not in this repo). It is a SvelteKit + Svelte + Vite chat app using `@json-render/svelte` that talks only to the `:8090` door (one generic `PluginService/CallMethod` over gRPC-Web, exactly one OIA1 or SID1 credential) and that op-web serves as static files from `/usr/local/share/op-dbus/dashboard/` — the dashboard root, `http://<host>:8080/`. The pinned release archive of that checkout is `vendor/3tched-json-render-ui`.

**Owner UI stack rule (2026-10-11):** implement application interfaces only
with Svelte/SvelteKit, Vite and json-render's Svelte renderer. This applies to
every user and chat mode, including generated interfaces. Every visible UI
element must be declared in the active catalog and implemented in its registry.
Installed skills for other frameworks are reference material only; they do
not authorize React/JSX/Next.js components,
another renderer, or framework dependencies in this application. Apply their
framework-independent guidance only where it fits this stack. The shared
UI-authoring preflight applies across modes; each caller keeps its existing
grants. Documentation availability never grants file or operation access.

```bash
# Build and deploy at op-web's root (from the UI repo)
cd /srv/git/3tched.com && LANDING=prod VITE_OPDBUS_DOOR=https://10.0.0.2:8090 npm run publish:op-web
cd /srv/git/3tched.com && URL_PREFIX=/ VITE_OPDBUS_DOOR=https://10.0.0.2:8090 npm run publish:op-web

# Dev server
cd /srv/git/3tched.com && npm run dev
```

A named mount is a separate directory under that root. op-web does **not** embed the UI via RustEmbed — it serves the deployed static files. There is no pairing. The current op-web identity endpoint refuses to infer a browser identity from a TCP source address; remote pickup uses the decoy issuer or an authenticated injecting host page.

On the configured HTTP pages at `10.0.0.2:8080` and `10.0.0.4:8080`, the UI uses op-web's existing same-origin Axum gRPC-Web connector, which forwards the unchanged identity metadata to the TLS door at `10.0.0.2:8090`. Other origins keep the direct HTTPS door. The generic `PluginService/CallMethod`, sealed capabilities, and interceptor identity checks remain the admission path; the connector does not mint or select an identity.

Fresh source exports also include the pinned UI source archive and verifier at
`vendor/3tched-json-render-ui/build-assets.sh`. That helper builds and checks the
captured UI without the sibling checkout or live rsync; golden preparation
stages only its validated asset archive and provenance manifest.

formatting checks and `/verify` run only when the owner explicitly requests
them; do not start them automatically before or after deployment. The owner
may assign those checks to a downtime agent. This supersedes the earlier

This includes disposable-VM tests and custom smoke fixtures. Do not make their
execution or repair a pre-installation/deployment gate. Further testing waits
until after deployment and an explicit owner request.

Perform the build required for the change and deploy only within the authorized
scope. Keep bounded operation receipts, safety checks and readiness evidence
separate from a test-suite pass; report built, installed, deployed and tested
status accurately. Do not repeat unchanged successful checks or turn a missing

name: typesafe-ai
license: MIT
description: >
  TypeSafe integration craft for System One models (sometimes called Decision Models) such as Jev,
  which answer typed questions about text, images, and application state with calibrated
  probabilities. Use when building, reviewing, or debugging code that calls TypeSafe; when writing
  its questions or state; when replacing an LLM prompt-and-parse step, keyword matching, or a
  brittle heuristic with a typed question; or when brainstorming where programmable common sense
10→  fits in an app.
---

# Build with TypeSafe

TypeSafe's **Jev**, the first public **System One model**, answers typed questions about state your
application supplies. State is the text, images, and application data your code sends with a
request. Jev can answer a Choice among options, a Noul (the probability that a statement is true), a
Score on levels you describe, or a Box that locates something in an image. Each answer comes back as
typed data with calibrated probabilities, for your code to use.
20→
The rest of this skill is guidance: patterns that tend to produce reliable integrations. None of it
is absolute. Models change, applications differ, and edge cases exist. When a situation calls for
something else, test the alternative and use your judgment.

## Judgments from Jev, decisions in code

Integrations tend to work best when Jev makes the judgments and code decides what to do with
them. Think of each decision as a **truth table**. Jev supplies the inputs, such as "Does the
customer sound frustrated?" or "Which product is the message about?". Code holds the logic that
30→maps those inputs to an action.

A question that asks Jev to make the decision, such as "Should this ticket be escalated?" or "What
should the agent do next?", usually means the question is at the wrong layer. Instead, break the
decision into the judgments it depends on, and write the decision itself in code, where it's
visible and testable. Writing out the table often shows gaps in the business logic too. A
combination of judgments with no defined outcome is a design question about the system, and it is
best settled in code.

## Live docs
40→
The live docs are the source of truth for request syntax, SDKs, question types, limits, and current
model behavior. Read the relevant pages as part of the task.

- Start at the [documentation index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt). Append `.md` to a page
  path to get the page as Markdown, and resolve relative links against `https://docs.typesafe.ai`.
- Exact request and response schemas: the [OpenAPI spec](https://api.typesafe.ai/openapi.json) and
  the [HTTP API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/api.md) page. For an SDK, see the
  [Python](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/python-sdk.md) or
  [JavaScript](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/js-sdk.md) page and the types in the installed package.
50→- Question types: [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/primitives.md) and each type's own page,
  [structured instructions and criteria](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/advanced.md), and
  [images](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/images.md).
- Models, context limits, and rate limits: [models](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/models.md). Known
  model weak spots and their workarounds are on the
  [jaggedness page](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/jaggedness.md).
- Architecture: [how to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/how-to-build.md),
  [patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/patterns.md), and
  [cookbooks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md). The cookbook closest to your use case is a
  good starting point for a new workflow.
60→
If you can't reach the live docs, use the installed SDK's types or local docs, and tell the user
you did. Leave out details that depend on the version rather than guessing them.

## Workflow

1. **Start from the decision logic.** Begin with what the application will show, select, change,
   or hand off. Sketch the truth table or rules that decide it, and list the inputs they need.
   Inputs that need an understanding of language or images make good questions. Arithmetic, dates,
   exact lookups, and policy usually belong in code. Aim for every question to feed the table, and
70→   give every combination of answers an outcome, including the case where a Noul lands between your
   thresholds. If code alone can already make the decision reliably, tell the user.
2. **Keep all question wording in one place.** Questions, options, criteria, and thresholds are the
   parts of an integration people audit and edit most. Keeping them together in one module makes
   that easier. [Design the state](#design-the-state) and
   [Write the questions](#write-the-questions) describe what tends to work.
3. **Probe the live API**: send test requests as described in
   [Test with the live API](#test-with-the-live-api). Use representative cases, hard cases, and
   negative cases. Keep going until the application behaves as intended.
4. **Integrate.** A few habits help here. Expose or log the exact request payload. When a call to
80→   the API fails, surface it as an error, not as an answer; for example, don't treat a failed call
   as a "no". Keep API keys on the server.

If the user's request is open-ended, offer the few directions from [Cookbooks](#cookbooks) that
best serve their goal, and recommend one. If the request is concrete, build it.

## Design the state

A useful check for any question is the **human test**: could a smart person, shown only this state
and this question, answer quickly by intuition? When a question fails the test, the fix is usually
90→in the state, not in the wording.

- **Give what a person would look at.** That means who sent each message, the full thread rather
  than a truncated last line, names rather than raw IDs or @-mention markup, and the item the
  question is about rather than the whole catalogue. State facts your code already knows, such as
  "all messages in `replies` were sent after the refund was issued", rather than leaving the model
  to work them out again.
- **Supply facts the model may lack**, such as what an internal product name or codename refers
  to.
- **Ensure every field in the state is relevant.** Irrelevant detail clutters the context and
100→  reduces accuracy. A field added for one question can sway the answer to another, and the model
  can read an empty list as a signal.
- **Be mindful when truncating.** Truncate long strings only when you need to, and check that the
  cut doesn't remove context the questions need.
- **Structure with named fields.** JSON objects with descriptive keys work better than a string of
  serialized JSON. They also let a question refer to each part by its path. Stable names such as
  `candidates.refund_policy` are easier to refer to than array positions.
- **Consider leaving out what no person could judge**, such as an unreadable crop or a distinction
  experts dispute. The model's answer there tends to be noise, and code will treat that noise as
  signal.
110→
## Write the questions

Break complex judgments or decisions into their parts, and combine the answers in code with
weighted sums, boolean logic, thresholds, or other heuristics to reach the final decision. For
example, rather than asking "Is this fraud?" or "Is this spam?", ask the set of atomic questions
about what might make something fraud or spam. Each question tends to work best when it asks for
**one judgment** that a person could make at a glance.

- **Ask the concrete, observable thing.** Aim for something a person could point to: "Is a SQL
120→  query built by string concatenation here?" rather than "Are there SQL injection risks?".
- **One judgment per question; beware the "or".** Two conditions joined by "or" or "and" usually
  work better as two questions. Likewise, a list of rules usually works better as one question per
  rule.
- **Anchor intent to the goal.** When the judgment is about what someone wants, it helps to name
  their goal: "Which of these files does the user want copied?" rather than "Which of these names
  the main input?".
- **Name the subject directly.** "Where is the coffee mug in `photo`?" reads better than "Where is
  `target` in `photo`?" with the target defined somewhere else. Context that only one question
  needs, including an image, usually fits best in that question's instructions (the question text)
130→  or its criteria (the descriptions of its options, its levels, or what yes and no mean). Context
  that many questions share can go in the state once, and each question can refer to it by its
  exact path in backticks. When you ask the same question about many items, it usually works better
  to put each item into its own question than to give an ID the model has to look up in a shared
  list.
- **Each question is answered on its own.** Questions in a request can't see each other or each
  other's answers. Any context a question relies on belongs in the state or in that question.
- **Write plainly.** A question isn't an LLM prompt. Preambles, "consider X, Y, and Z" lists, and
  output-format instructions add noise. Descriptions of the options belong in the criteria, not in
  the question. Phrase the question so that a true answer means yes. Watch for double negatives,
140→  and for presuppositions such as "the next step".
- **Name the case that causes confusion.** If answers keep mixing up two outcomes, say in the
  criteria what separates them, using the specific case. For example, for "Is this a refund
  request?", note that a question about the refund policy is not a request. A vague exclusion such
  as "not other kinds of message" helps less, and can draw attention to the wrong answer.

### Criteria

- **Ask about the null case separately.** A Box always returns a location and a Choice always picks
  an option, even when nothing fits. Pair either one with a Noul in the same request that asks
150→  whether anything fits ("Is there a coffee mug in `photo`?", "Does `message` name any of our
  products?"), so code can tell when nothing does. As of Jev 1.14, this companion Noul usually works
  better than a "none of the above" option.
- **Option names are sent to the model; question IDs are not.** Names that describe the content
  (`refund_request`, `shipping_delay`) help the model. Positional names (`A`, `left`, `option_1`)
  give it nothing meaningful to go on and can bias the answer.
- **Keep options distinct and concrete.** Wording that options share with each other, or with the
  input, can pull probability toward those options. An option that covers several meanings is
  often worth splitting, because its probability can't tell code which meaning applied. Direction
  and magnitude usually work better as separate questions, so that the answer to one doesn't get
160→  mixed into the other.
- **Describe each Score level as a situation.** Each level should make sense when read on its own:
  "The customer mentions a minor inconvenience" rather than "More upset than the previous level".
- **Describe a Noul's `false` criterion as a concrete situation**, such as "the package arrived on
  time", rather than as "not late".
- **Use a Noul per statement when more than one can be true.** A Choice picks one option, so a
  message that is both a refund request and a complaint forces it to split probability between the
  two. Separate Nouls let each one be true on its own.

## Compose requests
170→
**Bundle questions that share state.** A handy heuristic: if two calls would send the same state
with different questions, they can likely be one call. Questions are cheap and run in parallel, and
the state is read and paid for once. See
[parallel questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/parallel_questions.md).

**Ask speculatively**, meaning ask a question before you know whether you'll need its answer. A
question that only matters in some cases can go in the same request as the question that
identifies the case. Ask "Is `order` a return request?" and "Which item in `order.items` is being
returned?" together, and have code read the second answer only when the first is yes. The second
180→question doesn't need an "if" clause, because code handles the condition. See
[speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md).

A second request is usually worth it when:

- code needs an answer to build the next state, fetch evidence, or choose the next options;
- a state field needed for one question measurably misleads another;
- different sets of questions need to be cached or versioned separately.

## Read the answers
190→
### Confidence is rarely the gate

Naive implementations often use an answer's `confidence` as the check that decides whether code
acts. Confidence measures how concentrated an answer's probability distribution is, which is not
the same as how likely the answer is to be correct. Think about what the probabilities should look
like in your use case; another calculation over them may suit it better.

### Probabilities and thresholds

200→- **A probability is the likelihood that an answer is correct.** Jev isn't a calculator for
  probability problems. Ask it for judgments, and do any math on odds or probabilities in code. A
  Noul near 0.5 usually means the state doesn't settle the question.
- **The top answer is a good default**: the Choice's top option, or the Score's position.
- **0.7 and 0.3 make good starting thresholds for a Noul**: above 0.7 reads as yes, below 0.3 as no,
  and the band between means the question isn't settled, which can get its own row in the truth
  table. Adjust them when the application calls for it, and be wary of over-fitting them to a
  handful of test cases.
- **Look at Score distributions.** The Score's position can get pulled toward the middle and hide
  two-peaked answers, so look at the level probabilities before deciding which value your code
210→  reads.

## Test with the live API

Sending test requests to the live API is a great way to test questions against your data. Ask the
user for permission first. Get a budget for experimentation (TypeSafe is very inexpensive, so a
little can go a very long way), disclose what data will be sent (point out any personal or private
data), and say that their `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` will be used.

- Start with a few representative cases, plus hard ones and some whose answer is "no" or "nothing
220→  fits".
- Compare wordings by sending each variant as a separate question in one request, over the same
  state.
- Read individual answers, not only aggregates.
- Keep the exact request payload for each case so any result can be rerun.
- Check each change against cases you didn't use while tuning.

Make sure any agent that sends test requests has network access to the API endpoint.

### When an answer looks wrong
230→
Check these, in this order:

1. the payload as actually sent;
2. the state, against the human test;
3. the options and candidates: is the right answer among them?
4. the scope of the questions: can each one be broken down into smaller judgments?
5. the wording.

If a clear question with complete state still gets an answer you're confident is wrong, check the
240→jaggedness page for the model you're using. It lists known weak spots and how to work around them.
If the behavior isn't listed, the TypeSafe team welcomes examples through the channel linked on
that page. In the meantime, work out an alternative approach with the user that avoids the weak
spot.

### Yellow flags

Typically, a good change is one that makes the definition clearer or improves the state. Check each
change on cases you didn't tune on. Wording written to produce a particular value is **prompt
gymnastics**, and it tends to break on new inputs and on the next model version. Some yellow flags:
250→
- criteria that name specific test items, or that gain a clause for each failing case;
- caveats that explain away a model quirk;
- thresholds fitted to particular cases;
- tests that assert an exact probability;
- code that quietly overrides answers.

The structural fix is usually better state, a separate question, or code.

## Cookbooks
260→
Each of these starting points combines questions to serve one goal. Ideas outside this list are
welcome.

- **Route and fill arguments.** One request identifies what the user is asking for and which
  values go in each argument. Code then calls the handler. See
  [function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md) and
  [intent routing](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/intent-routing.md).
- **Select instead of generate.** Code finds candidate values or spans of text, the model picks
  the intended one, and code copies or normalizes it. See
270→  [value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md),
  [date extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/date_extraction_cookbook.md), and
  [structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md).
- **Find and judge evidence.** Retrieve candidates and ask how relevant each one is. See
  [line-by-line search](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/semantic_find.md),
  [re-ranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md), and
  [classifying RAG passages](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/classifying_rag_passages.md).
- **Turn answers into data.** Score each dimension once, then let code or users change the weights
  and views. If you have labeled outcomes, the answers can become features for a model. See
  [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) and
280→  [feature discovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery.md).
- **Verify and escalate.** Check claims or fields against their evidence, and send the cases that
  fail to a person or a reasoning model. See
  [citation checks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md) and
  [extraction cascades](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md).

The TypeSafe team is constantly adding cookbooks of well-tested patterns to the live documentation.
It's a good idea to check the [cookbooks index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md) for one
that fits the problem you're solving.

# Rust

## Overview

Rust is a systems programming language focused on safety, concurrency, and performance. The ownership system guarantees memory safety without garbage collection, and the type system enforces thread safety at compile time.
20→
**When to use:** Systems programming, web services (axum), CLI tools (clap), terminal UIs (ratatui), WebAssembly, performance-critical applications, anything requiring memory safety without runtime overhead.

**When NOT to use:** Rapid prototyping where compile times matter more than safety, simple scripting tasks, projects where the team has no Rust experience and deadlines are tight.

## Quick Reference

| Pattern             | API / Tool                          | Key Points                           |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Ownership transfer  | `let b = a;`                        | `a` is moved, no longer usable       |
30→| Borrowing           | `&T` / `&mut T`                     | One mutable OR many immutable refs   |
| Lifetime annotation | `fn f<'a>(x: &'a str) -> &'a str`   | Ties output lifetime to input        |
| Error propagation   | `?` operator                        | Converts and propagates errors       |
| Custom errors       | `thiserror::Error` derive           | Structured error types with Display  |
| Ad-hoc errors       | `anyhow::Result<T>`                 | Context chaining for applications    |
| Async runtime       | `#[tokio::main]`                    | Entry point for async programs       |
| Spawn task          | `tokio::spawn(async { })`           | Concurrent async task execution      |
| HTTP router         | `axum::Router::new().route(...)`    | Composable routing with extractors   |
| Extractors          | `Json<T>`, `Path<T>`, `State<T>`    | Type-safe request parsing            |
| Serialization       | `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` | serde with format-agnostic derives   |
40→| CLI parsing         | `#[derive(Parser)]`                 | clap derive API for arg parsing      |
| TUI rendering       | `terminal.draw(\|f\| { })`          | Immediate-mode ratatui rendering     |
| Benchmarking        | `criterion::Criterion`              | Statistical benchmarking framework   |
| Dep auditing        | `cargo deny check`                  | License, vulnerability, source audit |
| Binary release      | `cargo dist init`                   | Cross-platform binary distribution   |
| Changelog           | `release-plz update`                | Auto semver bump and changelog       |

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake                                 | Correct Pattern                               |
50→| --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Returning reference to local variable   | Return owned type or use lifetime parameter   |
| Using `unwrap()` in library code        | Return `Result` and let caller decide         |
| `clone()` to satisfy borrow checker     | Restructure code to avoid the borrow conflict |
| Blocking in async context               | Use `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`             |
| Shared mutable state without sync       | Use `Arc<Mutex<T>>` or channels               |
| `String` where `&str` suffices          | Accept `&str` in function parameters          |
| Ignoring `must_use` warnings            | Handle or explicitly discard with `let _ =`   |
| Large enum variants                     | Box the large variant to reduce overall size  |
| `async fn` in traits without bounds     | Add `Send` bound or use `async-trait` crate   |
60→| Missing `#[tokio::test]` on async tests | Use `#[tokio::test]` instead of `#[test]`     |

# MCP Expert

## Overview

Definitive resource for building and managing Model Context Protocol ecosystems. Covers the full lifecycle from server development and transport configuration to security, elicitation, and async task execution. Designs agent-first tool interfaces that minimize token usage and maximize LLM accuracy.

**When to use:** Building MCP servers, designing tool interfaces, configuring transports (Stdio/Streamable HTTP), implementing OAuth 2.1, troubleshooting connectivity, using elicitation for server-initiated user interaction.

**When NOT to use:** Application-level business logic, non-MCP API design, frontend UI components, general HTTP API development unrelated to MCP.

## Quick Reference

| Pattern                | API/Approach                             | Key Points                                        |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Outcome-oriented tools | Single-call operations                   | Avoid chatty multi-step APIs                      |
| Argument flattening    | Flat Zod schemas with descriptions       | Reduce model hallucination                        |
| Progressive disclosure | Return `mcp://` URIs for large data      | Agent reads partially via `resources/read`        |
| Retryable tools        | Return `retry_with` suggestions          | Help LLM self-correct on bad inputs               |
| Helpful errors         | Descriptive strings with fix guidance    | Never return raw exceptions or stack traces       |
30→| Pagination             | `has_more` + `next_cursor` metadata      | 20-50 records per call maximum                    |
| Structured outputs     | JSON Schema in `outputSchema`            | Typed tool results for programmatic consumption   |
| Stdio transport        | Local tools, stderr-only logging         | Never write to stdout except JSON-RPC             |
| Streamable HTTP        | Remote/cloud tools, single endpoint      | Replaces deprecated SSE transport                 |
| OAuth 2.1 with PKCE    | Enterprise data access                   | MCP server is resource server, not auth server    |
| Elicitation            | Server-initiated user input              | Flat schema maps to forms, three response states  |
| Async tasks            | `tasks/get`, `tasks/cancel`              | Long-running operations return task handles       |
| Capability scopes      | `read:docs`, `write:code`, `admin:users` | Granular permission boundaries                    |
| HITL gate              | `confirmation_required` flag             | Manual approval for destructive actions           |
| URL elicitation        | Secure credential collection             | Redirects user to browser for sensitive input     |
40→| Extensions             | Namespaced capability negotiation        | Optional features without forking the spec        |
| Sampling with tools    | Server-initiated LLM requests            | Enables server-side agent loops                   |
| MCP Inspector          | `npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector`    | Test tools interactively without an LLM           |
| Unit testing           | InMemoryTransport + Vitest               | Test tool handlers with mock client               |
| Evaluation framework   | Schema, error, pagination assertions     | Validate tool quality for LLM consumption         |
| Tool contract testing  | Schema field descriptions, edge cases    | Every field described, optional params handled    |
| CI smoke tests         | GitHub Actions + Inspector CLI           | Automated build, test, and transport health check |

## Spec Versions

50→The current MCP specification is **2025-11-25**. Key milestones:

- **2025-03-26**: Streamable HTTP transport (deprecated standalone SSE), tool annotations
- **2025-06-18**: Structured tool outputs, elicitation, OAuth auth server separation
- **2025-11-25**: Async tasks, extensions framework, sampling with tools, CIMD auth, server discovery

## Onboarding Protocol

When an agent needs a new capability:

60→1. **Validation**: Check if the required MCP server is already active
2. **Guide**: If missing, provide the user with a direct installation path
3. **Config**: Use `uvx` or `npx` for zero-install execution where possible

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake                                              | Correct Pattern                                                             |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Designing chatty APIs requiring many round-trips     | Build outcome-oriented tools that accomplish tasks in a single call         |
| Logging to stdout breaking the Stdio transport       | Log only to stderr to keep the transport channel clean                      |
70→| Returning raw exceptions and stack traces to the LLM | Return helpful error strings with suggested corrections                     |
| Building monolithic servers with dozens of tools     | Keep servers focused with 5-15 tools for discoverability and maintenance    |
| Using deprecated HTTP+SSE transport for new servers  | Use Streamable HTTP for remote servers (single endpoint, optional SSE)      |
| Hardcoding secrets in MCP server configuration       | Use environment variable mapping for all sensitive values                   |
| Returning large datasets in a single tool call       | Use pagination (20-50 records) or resource URIs for large data              |
| Implementing auth server inside MCP server           | MCP server acts as OAuth 2.1 resource server only, delegate auth externally |
| Vague tool descriptions causing LLM hallucination    | Add example usage and strict constraints to the tool description field      |
| Synchronous blocking on long operations              | Return async task handles for operations exceeding timeout thresholds       |
| Passing received tokens to upstream APIs             | Validate tokens locally; never forward to avoid confused deputy attacks     |
| Requesting secrets through elicitation               | Use URL mode elicitation or dedicated OAuth flows for credential collection |
80→
## MCP Primitives

MCP servers expose three core primitive types to clients:

- **Tools**: Model-controlled actions the LLM invokes to accomplish tasks (function calling)
- **Resources**: Application-controlled data exposed via `mcp://` URIs that clients read on demand
- **Prompts**: User-controlled templates that provide structured context for specific workflows

Servers declare which primitives they support during capability negotiation in the `initialize` handshake. The November 2025 spec adds **Tasks** as an experimental primitive for async execution.
90→
## Transport Selection

| Scenario             | Transport       | Notes                                                   |
| -------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| Local CLI tools      | Stdio           | Fastest startup, no network overhead                    |
| Remote/cloud servers | Streamable HTTP | Single endpoint, optional SSE streaming                 |
| Legacy remote        | HTTP+SSE        | Deprecated since 2025-03-26, migrate to Streamable HTTP |

Clients should support Stdio whenever possible. Streamable HTTP supports both stateless and stateful server implementations via optional `Mcp-Session-Id` headers.

# Security

Security is built-in, not bolted-on. Every feature, endpoint, and data flow must consider security implications.

## OWASP Top 10 (2025)

| #   | Vulnerability                      | Prevention                                      |
| --- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | Broken Access Control              | Verify permissions server-side, default deny    |
20→| 2   | Security Misconfiguration          | Secure defaults, remove unused features         |
| 3   | Software Supply Chain Failures     | SBOM, dependency scanning, signed builds        |
| 4   | Cryptographic Failures             | Use TLS, hash passwords (argon2id), encrypt PII |
| 5   | Injection                          | Parameterized queries, input validation         |
| 6   | Insecure Design                    | Threat modeling, security requirements          |
| 7   | Authentication Failures            | Strong passwords, MFA, secure session mgmt      |
| 8   | Software or Data Integrity         | Verify dependencies, sign releases              |
| 9   | Logging and Alerting Failures      | Log security events, set up alerts              |
| 10  | Mishandling Exceptional Conditions | Fail securely, generic errors to clients        |

30→## Security Principles

| Principle          | Rule                                                      |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Defense in Depth   | Multiple layers: firewall, auth, authz, encryption, audit |
| Least Privilege    | Minimum permissions needed, nothing more                  |
| Zero Trust         | Never trust, always verify. Assume breach.                |
| Secure by Default  | HTTPS, strict passwords, secure cookies out of the box    |
| Fail Securely      | Access denied on error, no internal details to users      |
| Validate on Server | Client validation is UX, server validation is security    |
40→
## Pre-Deployment Checklist

| Area          | Requirements                                                        |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Passwords     | Hashed with argon2id (preferred) or bcrypt (12+ rounds)             |
| Tokens        | JWT with EdDSA/ES256, 15min access / 7d refresh, httpOnly cookies   |
| Sessions      | HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookies                           |
| Rate Limiting | Auth endpoints: 5 attempts/15min                                    |
| Authorization | All routes check auth server-side, default deny                     |
50→| Input         | Validated with schema (Zod), parameterized SQL                      |
| Uploads       | Whitelist types, enforce size limits                                |
| Secrets       | No secrets in code or VCS                                           |
| Headers       | CSP (with nonces), HSTS, Permissions-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options |
| CORS          | Configured restrictively                                            |
| Encryption    | PII encrypted at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.3)            |
| Logging       | Audit logging for security events                                   |
| Dependencies  | SBOM generated, `npm audit` clean, Dependabot enabled               |

## Threat Modeling (STRIDE)
60→
| Threat                 | Category        | Key Mitigations                                        |
| ---------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Spoofing               | Authentication  | MFA, strong passwords, JWT with short expiry           |
| Tampering              | Integrity       | Input validation, HTTPS/TLS, signed tokens             |
| Repudiation            | Accountability  | Audit logging, digital signatures                      |
| Info Disclosure        | Confidentiality | Encryption, least privilege, secret management         |
| Denial of Service      | Availability    | Rate limiting, input validation, CDN/DDoS protection   |
| Elevation of Privilege | Authorization   | Authz checks on every request, ABAC, permission audits |

70→## Risk Levels

| Level    | Action                    |
| -------- | ------------------------- |
| Critical | Immediate action required |
| High     | Address before launch     |
| Medium   | Address post-launch       |
| Low      | Monitor, may accept risk  |

## Compliance Overview
80→
| Framework | Scope              | Key Requirements                                                   |
| --------- | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| GDPR      | EU data subjects   | Consent, data subject rights, breach notification (72h), DPIA      |
| HIPAA     | US healthcare data | PHI encryption, RBAC, audit logs, BAA with providers               |
| SOC 2     | SaaS customer data | Security policies, MFA, encryption, incident response              |
| PCI-DSS   | Credit card data   | Use payment processor (Stripe), tokenization, network segmentation |

## Anti-Patterns

90→| Anti-Pattern                                  | Fix                                              |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Security as afterthought                      | Integrate from design phase                      |
| Client-side authorization                     | Always verify permissions server-side            |
| Trusting client data (e.g., userId from body) | Get user ID from authenticated session           |
| Rolling your own crypto                       | Use proven libraries (argon2, bcrypt, libsodium) |
| Compliance = security                         | Compliance is the minimum; security is ongoing   |
| Verbose error responses                       | Generic messages to clients, details server-side |

## Common Mistakes
100→
| Mistake                                                       | Correct Pattern                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Performing authorization checks only on the client side       | Always verify permissions server-side; client checks are UX only    |
| Trusting user-supplied IDs from request body (e.g., userId)   | Derive user identity from the authenticated session or token        |
| Rolling custom cryptography instead of using proven libraries | Use argon2id, bcrypt, or libsodium for all cryptographic operations |
| Treating compliance certification as equivalent to security   | Compliance is the minimum bar; security requires ongoing review     |
| Returning verbose error messages with stack traces to clients | Show generic messages to clients; log details server-side only      |

- **Implement authentication, authorization, and security headers end-to-end**: Use `Task` agent to configure JWT, RBAC, CSP, HSTS, and rate limiting
